entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

I'm still drafting more edge-case titles: renamed Evidence not getting a source reference until republished, Sources mentioned only in passing text staying inert, one Source's title being a substring of another's not causing false links, and renaming the Source node type itself.

For rejected cases I'm phrasing them as untouched-state outcomes—Evidence whose Source never publishes stays as-is, and publishing just a Claim triggers nothing. Then I'm sketching the pass conditions for each check, like Evidence starting with no source reference, later pointing to the correct Source primary key, and other Evidence entries remaining unaffected.

I'm going through more edge cases: a renamed node keeping its original title with no source reference, a claim lacking a source reference alongside a missing notes page, and various source-reference mismatches like appendix versus base title, renamed node types, and batch-published evidence—checking that each resolves to the correct source name.

I'm also refining the claim about publishing a Source from Roam: it should only set source references on Evidence that lacks one, skip anything else, and warn when an Evidence's Source isn't in the space while still storing no reference. Then I'm setting up the given scenario—a signed-in Roam graph with node sharing on and sync off in the eng-2329-demo group, containing one Source, two Evidence nodes naming it, and a third Evidence node naming a second unpublished Source, none of which exist in the database yet.

entries.name: SendMessage
entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

# MANDATORY RULES — Check every session

## NEVER add Co-Authored-By
Never add `Co-Authored-By` lines to commits. All commits are sid's. No exceptions.

## NEVER cd out of the worktree
When the env says `Primary working directory: .../.claude/worktrees/<TICKET>`, all commands stay inside it. Bash cwd persists, and absolute `Edit` paths to `/mnt/data/projects/discourse-graph/apps/roam/...` silently target the MAIN repo on `main`. Use `git -C <worktree>` or `(cd ...; cmd)` subshells; never bare `cd` to the main repo path. See [[feedback_stay_in_worktree]].

## NEVER use git reset --hard
`git reset --hard` destroys untracked files that were accidentally staged in a prior commit.
Use `git restore` or `git checkout -- <file>` for targeted resets. If you absolutely must
reset, stash or back up untracked files first. NEVER run `git reset --hard` without asking.

## Ticket is the spec, code is the source of truth
The Linear ticket (description + comments) is the spec. The code is the source of truth for current behavior. Anything neither settles goes to sid as a question with a proposed default. Never read Roam design blocks, worklog pages, or other upstream traces to fill a gap unless sid names the UID in this conversation, even if a launcher or memory lists them as "read first". See [[feedback-ticket-is-spec-code-is-truth]].

## NEVER assume, ALWAYS look up
When the user references something by name ("accessors", "the helper", "that util", etc.):
1. **STOP. Do NOT assume you know what they mean from conversation context.**
2. **Search the codebase** (Grep/Glob) for the actual thing they're referencing.
3. Only proceed after you've read the actual code.

This applies especially when the user says "we already have X for that" — go find X before writing anything.

## ALWAYS run all three checks after changes
From `apps/roam/` (or worktree equivalent):
1. `npx eslint --max-warnings 0 <changed-files>`
2. `npx prettier --check <changed-files>`
3. `npx tsc --noEmit --skipLibCheck`

All three must pass. Don't skip `tsc` — example/test files reference exported types and will break on schema changes.

## PR workflow skills (2026-08-31, supersedes the michael-trio rule)
The old trio (/think-like-michael, /review-like-michael, /save-from-myself) is SUPERSEDED — /pre-pr-review covers them. Do not run the trio per PR anymore. Standing set:

**Per PR:**
1. `/pre-pr-review` — independent Opus pass, after push and after follow-up pushes (implementer self-review doesn't count)
2. `scope-check` — after review; produces the `## Scope check` section for the PR body (team template `.github/pull_request_template.md`)
3. `pr-video` — only if the PR is missing a demo for the template's Loom section

**During implementation:** `roam-global-tailwind` when styling Roam UI.
**Team-facing prose:** `dg-engineering-writing-style` always; tickets via `dg-create-engineering-ticket`.
**Never** use `ask-as-sid` on this project.
Curt directives ("minimal commit push") still skip the per-PR skills — see [[feedback_minimal_means_skip_skills]]. Details: [[feedback-pr-workflow-skills]].

## Follow findings to their conclusion
When reviewing code (especially during skill passes), if you observe facts that together imply a problem, STATE the problem. Don't list observations and move on.
- Trace return types through every call site. If a function always returns `T` (never undefined), then `?? fallback` is dead code at that site — even if other sites need it.
- "Unnecessary" = "remove it." Don't soften to "not harmful."
- "Consistent with other sites" is not a reason to keep dead code.

## Minimize reviewer cognitive load
- Don't rearrange existing code unnecessarily.
- Don't extract variables that are only used once.
- Keep diffs minimal: only change what's needed for the task.

entries.name: WebFetch
entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

Two tooling gotchas that silently dropped outward actions on 2026-09-16.

- `gh pr edit <n> --body-file … / --add-reviewer …` exits 1 on DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph with "GraphQL: Projects (classic) is being deprecated … (repository.pullRequest.projectCards)" and applies nothing. Use the REST API instead: `gh api -X PATCH repos/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pulls/<n> -F body=@file` and `gh api -X POST repos/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pulls/<n>/requested_reviewers -f 'reviewers[]=<login>'`. `gh pr comment`, `gh pr merge`, `gh pr view` are unaffected.
- In zsh, `git push origin $sha:refs/heads/$branch` is parsed as the `:r` modifier on `$sha`, producing `<sha>efs/heads/...` and "src refspec does not match any". Always write `"${sha}:refs/heads/${branch}"`, and verify with `git ls-remote` after the push, not from the shell exit code.

**Why:** both failures print an error but the surrounding script kept going, so a batch reported "pushed" / "updated" while the remote was untouched.
**How to apply:** for any outward gh/git batch, verify the remote state afterwards (ls-remote head, `gh pr view --json body/reviewRequests`) instead of trusting the command sequence. Related: [[feedback_prefer_api_over_browser]].

# MANDATORY RULES — Check every session
- **NEVER add Co-Authored-By** to commits. All commits are sid's. No exceptions.
- **NEVER cd out of the worktree.** When the env says `Primary working directory: .../.claude/worktrees/<TICKET>`, all commands stay inside it; absolute `Edit` paths to `/mnt/data/projects/discourse-graph/apps/roam/...` silently target MAIN on `main`. Use `git -C <worktree>` or `(cd ...; cmd)` subshells. See [[feedback_stay_in_worktree]].
- **NEVER use `git reset --hard`** without asking: it destroys untracked files that were accidentally staged earlier. Use `git restore` / `git checkout -- <file>`; back up untracked files first if a reset is unavoidable.
- **Ticket is the spec, code is the source of truth.** Anything neither settles goes to sid as a question with a proposed default. Never read Roam design blocks, worklog pages or other upstream traces to fill a gap unless sid names the UID in this conversation, even if a launcher or memory lists them. See [[feedback-ticket-is-spec-code-is-truth]].
- **NEVER assume, ALWAYS look up.** When sid names something ("accessors", "the helper", "we already have X"), stop, search the codebase, read the actual code, then proceed.
- **ALWAYS run all three checks after changes** (from `apps/roam/` or the worktree): `npx eslint --max-warnings 0 <files>`, `npx prettier --check <files>`, `npx tsc --noEmit --skipLibCheck`. All must pass; never skip `tsc` (examples and tests reference exported types).
- **PR workflow skills** (2026-08-31; they supersede the michael trio). Per PR: `/pre-pr-review` (an independent Opus pass after each push), then `scope-check` (the PR body's `## Scope check`), then `pr-video` only if the Loom section lacks a demo. During implementation: `roam-global-tailwind` for Roam UI. Team prose: `dg-engineering-writing-style`; tickets via `dg-create-engineering-ticket`. Never `ask-as-sid` here. Curt directives ("minimal commit push") skip the per-PR skills: [[feedback_minimal_means_skip_skills]], [[feedback-pr-workflow-skills]].
- **Follow findings to their conclusion.** If facts imply a problem, state it. Trace return types through every call site (`?? fallback` on a value that is never undefined is dead code there). "Unnecessary" means remove it; "consistent with other sites" is no reason to keep dead code.
- **Minimize reviewer cognitive load.** Don't rearrange code unnecessarily, don't extract single-use variables, keep diffs to what the task needs.

content.text:
You're right, and my reply to maparent was wrong to call it "expected". Here's how it fits together.

**What each PR does**
- **ENG-2293** (#1473, merged 09-23, the import side): when you import an Evidence, it follows the Evidence's stored source reference and imports the Source too. It can only follow a reference that's actually stored.
- **ENG-2329** (this PR, the publish side): if the Evidence was published before its Source, publishing it stored *no* reference, so 2293 had nothing to follow. That's the original bug. This PR fills in the missing stored reference when the Source is published later.

**Why maparent still sees `[[@placeholder]]`**
- Their Evidence copy was imported *before* the Source was published, so it correctly got the placeholder at that point.
- After this PR restores the reference, re-importing that copy gets skipped. The import decides "already up to date" by comparing modified times only (`materializeSharedNode.ts:88-99` and `:431-445`).
- Restoring the reference deliberately doesn't change the modified time. Bumping it would make importers skip a later real edit.
- Nothing on the import side notices that a source has since appeared. Only the per-page Refresh button, which skips that check, fixes it.

**Against Done When 1:** it says that after publishing Evidence and then its Source, "importing that Evidence imports the Source and resolves the title without the warning." maparent re-imported after the Source was published and got a skip. By the plain words, that fails Done When 1. I drew the line where the code stopped, not where the ticket does.

**The fix: one check on the import side, in this PR.** When the local copy still has `[[@placeholder]]` and the shared Evidence now has a source reference, don't skip it as up to date. Re-import and "Refresh all" would then rebuild the title, and 2293's logic would import the Source along with it. It's about 5 lines plus a test in `materializeSharedNode.ts`. It doesn't bump modified times, so it doesn't bring back the lost-edit problem.

**Separate, and not in any ticket:** maparent also expected that importing *only the Source* would fix their existing Evidence copy, with no re-import. That means scanning existing imports whenever a Source is imported. Done When 1 doesn't ask for it, so it would be a follow-up ticket if you want it.

My recommendation is to add the import-side check to this PR, then correct my reply to maparent. Should I go ahead?

- **The skip check:** an up-to-date copy is skipped only if that helper is false. So re-import and "DG: Refresh all imported nodes" now rebuild a placeholder copy once its Source exists, instead of skipping it.

- **New:** a placeholder copy that's otherwise up to date gets re-imported and renamed to `[[EVD]] - … - [[@Smith 2020]]`. It fails with the fix disabled.
- **Changed:** "does not look up the source of an import that is up to date". It used to assert that no page title is read at all. It now allows exactly one read, of the imported page's own title, and still pins that the Source isn't looked up.

**What it costs:** one local Roam title read per up-to-date import that has a source reference. There's no extra database call.

content.content:
`core/database.ts` holds the address; every path in proof uses it.
- **A checkout's schema.** `db.ts up` writes `proof/db/supabase/` from
  `discourse-graph/packages/database/supabase` (config, migrations, schemas)
  and brings the database to those migrations: new ones apply in place, and
  when one it applied changed or is gone (switching from a PR's worktree back
  to main) it resets. `--from <worktree>` tests a PR's own migrations.
- **Seeded with what kits name.** The dev graph (space 66566) and the
  Obsidian test vault (106039) as publish sources, test-3-graph (120237), each
  with its anonymous account, the authors 3 and 106041, and the
  `eng-2329-demo` group all three are in. Generated ids start at 200000.

```bash
DB="npx tsx /mnt/data/projects/dg-demo-videos/proof/db.ts"
$DB up [--from <checkout>]   # start, migrate, seed, write proof/db/.env
$DB status                   # answering? which checkout's schema?
$DB reset                    # back to the migrations, seeded again
- A fixture without a check runs every time. Use that for settings Roam resets
  on each load.
- `rest` reaches the proof database's REST API with `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`.
- `{ "publish": { space, author, group, types, nodes } }` (outside) writes
  what another space's publish would have: node types (`{ id, label, format,
  template? }`), nodes (`{ id, type, title, body? }`) with their Document and
  direct and full Content rows, and ResourceAccess for the group. The
  space's platform picks the shapes Roam or Obsidian write. It's all upserts,
  so leave out the check and it runs on every take. test-3-graph is in the
  `eng-2329-demo` group with the dev graph (space 66566, author 3) and the
  Obsidian test vault (space 106039, author 106041), so either can be the
  source.
- The proof database runs without edge functions, so a Roam kit that touches
  the database signs in before load: the `database-session` fixture in the
  shipped kits runs `proof.supabase.signIn({ serviceKey, publishableKey })`.
  It makes what create-space would have (the graph's Space row, its
  anonymous account with the password the graph stores, PlatformAccount and
  editor access) and writes the session the extension reads. Its check,
  `proof.supabase.signedIn()`, asks the proof database whether it knows the
  session's user, so a session from another stack (DG keys every local one
  `sb-127:`) or from before a reset signs in again.
- Name what a kit creates with `{{ns}}` (the kit's namespace) so cleanup can
  find it and kits don't collide in a shared test graph.

no-earlier-import: neither node type nor node was imported into this graph before
